Icons: a sign for the taint, a badge for the toleration, a magnet or label tag for the selector. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: a taint keeps other pods out, a toleration only allows entry, and a selector is what pulls the pod to the right pool.
alt: A taint repels pods without a toleration, a toleration alone does not attract a pod, and a node selector sends it to the right GPU pool.
cap: A taint keeps out pods without a toleration, but only a node selector steers a GPU pod to the right pool.

name: k19-checkpoint-drain
title: Draining a node that runs a training job
spec: A left-to-right row of four numbered steps joined by arrows, drawn as four lanes of work. Step 1 box, labelled Platform marks the job as needing a checkpoint, with a flag icon. Step 2 box, labelled Job writes its state to shared storage and says it is done, with a disk cylinder icon for shared storage. Step 3 box, labelled Platform drains the node, so the pods stop and release the hardware, with a gear icon. Step 4 box, labelled Job scheduler starts the job again on a healthy node, and the job loads the checkpoint it just wrote, with a clock or restart icon. Number circles 1 to 4 (r=24, green, white numbers) sit on the step boxes. Under step 2 and step 4, a small note reads checkpoint. Orange note under the whole row: the job loses only the work done since its last checkpoint. Green takeaway bar: checkpoint first, drain second, restart on a healthy node.
alt: Four steps move a training job off a node being drained: checkpoint, save state, drain, and restart from the checkpoint elsewhere.
cap: A training job is checkpointed before its node is drained, so it restarts elsewhere and loses only recent work.

name: k19-capi-pivot
title: Hub-and-spoke autoscaling versus a pivoted workload cluster
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel titled Hub and spoke: a box at the top labelled Management cluster, containing the Cluster and MachineDeployment objects. A downward arrow from it into a lower box labelled Workload cluster, which contains Cluster Autoscaler. The arrow is orange and labelled needs the management cluster to scale out during peak load. Right panel titled Pivoted (self-contained): a box labelled Workload cluster that contains three items: Cluster API controllers, its own Cluster and Machine resources, and Cluster Autoscaler. A dashed arrow from a smaller box labelled Management cluster points into the workload cluster and is labelled start cluster creation and deletion. A label inside the right panel reads day-to-day autoscaling and local controller lookups stay on the local API server. Gear icons for controllers, a window icon for the autoscaler. Green takeaway bar: keep the scale-out loop local, and let the hub only start and delete clusters.
alt: In a hub-and-spoke layout the workload cluster depends on a management cluster to scale out; in a pivoted layout the controllers run inside the workload cluster.
cap: A pivoted Cluster API setup lets the workload cluster scale on its own, while the management cluster only starts and deletes clusters.

name: k19-etcd-scale
title: Worker node count sets when etcd moves to dedicated machines
spec: A horizontal scale line from left to right labelled worker nodes, with three marked points: 50 at the first mark, 200 at the second. Segment one, from 0 to 50, shaded light green, labelled colocated etcd is fine: kubeadm runs it as static pods, saving management overhead and infrastructure cost. Segment two, from 50 to 200, shaded pale orange, labelled consider dedicated etcd machines, because etcd competes with kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager for resources. Segment three, past 200, labelled plan for dedicated etcd clusters from the start. Under the segment three, a box of three requirements with icons: fast local disks for etcd, low-latency links within the region, and no load balancer between kube-apiserver and etcd. An arrow beside the last requirement points from kube-apiserver to etcd, crossed out with an orange mark, labelled connects to each member directly. Green takeaway bar: the bigger the cluster, the earlier etcd needs its own machines.
anchor: ### Dedicated versus colocated etcd and node pool sizing ratios
alt: Colocated etcd is fine up to 50 worker nodes, dedicated etcd is considered past 50, and planned from the start past 200.
cap: Etcd can run on the control-plane machines for small clusters, but it moves to dedicated machines as the worker count passes 50 and 200.

name: k20-skew-ladder
title: Version skew: how far each component may lag the API server
spec: A vertical ladder of stacked boxes, top to bottom, with the kube-apiserver at the top as the reference. The top box is a large green box labelled kube-apiserver at n, with a second smaller box beside it labelled HA kube-apiserver instances at n and n-1 during a rolling upgrade. Below it, a row of boxes, each with a short arrow pointing up toward the API server: kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler and cloud-controller-manager, labelled may be up to one minor older, never newer. Next row: kubelet and kube-proxy, labelled up to three minors older (two before 1.28), never newer. A separate box off to one side, joined by a double-headed arrow to the API server: kubectl, labelled one minor away in either direction, n-1 to n+1. Each box has a small icon: a gear for controllers, a window for kubectl, a chip for kubelet. The orange highlight marks one arrow or label only: never newer than kube-apiserver. Numbered steps 1 and 2 beside the ladder show the order: 1 upgrade the control plane, 2 upgrade the nodes one minor at a time. Green takeaway bar: every component may lag, none may run ahead of the API server.
alt: Version skew ladder: the API server is the reference, and controllers, kubelets and kubectl may lag within set limits but never run ahead.
cap: Each component may lag the API server by a set number of minors, but none may run ahead of it.

name: k20-restore-decision
title: Replace a member or restore a snapshot: decide by quorum
spec: A top-down decision flow. Start box at the top labelled A member has failed, or the data needs recovery, with a warning icon. Below it a diamond-shaped decision box labelled Does a majority of etcd members still answer? Two arrows leave the diamond. The left arrow, labelled Yes, leads to a green box labelled A. Replace the member: run member remove on the dead ID, then rebuild the node with kubeadm join --control-plane, then check endpoint health --cluster. The right arrow, labelled No, leads to a box labelled B. Restore from snapshot: stop kube-apiserver and etcd on all control-plane nodes, run etcdutl snapshot restore on each node with its own name and peer URL, restore etcd first and then kube-apiserver. Under box B, a small grey note: corrupted data also goes to B. Number steps 1 to 3 inside box B are optional; use the three phases stop, restore, restart. Orange note beside the Yes arrow: replace instead of restoring when quorum is intact. Green takeaway bar: check quorum first, because that answer decides between replacing a member and restoring from a snapshot. Monospace labels for etcdctl and etcdutl commands.
alt: If a majority of etcd members still answers, replace the broken member; if not, restore from a snapshot.
cap: Whether a majority of etcd members still answers decides between replacing one member and restoring the whole cluster from a snapshot.

name: k20-quorum-trap
title: Replacing a dedicated etcd member: subtractive versus additive
spec: Three horizontal rows, each a short sequence of boxes with arrows left to right. Each box is a round node with a small etcd member icon and a voting count label. Row 1, titled Subtractive, 3 to 2 to 3: box one shows three voting members, all healthy. Box two shows one member removed with etcdctl member remove and its host terminated, leaving two voting members with quorum of 2 and zero fault tolerance for the 10 to 15 minutes the replacement takes to boot and sync. Box three shows the replacement joins and the cluster is back to three. The second box is outlined in orange with a label: a disk stall or network blip on either remaining node loses quorum for the whole control plane. Row 2, titled Additive learner, 3 to 4 learner to promote to remove old to 3: box one shows the new upgraded node added as a learner, which receives data but does not vote; box two shows it promoted, giving four members with three needed for quorum; box three shows the old node removed, leaving three voting members. A green label under row 2 reads three healthy voting members stay active throughout. Row 3, titled In-place rolling upgrade: one box labelled upgrade one member at a time, with the other two members staying online, drawn as three small members with one highlighted. Green takeaway bar: keep three healthy voting members through every replacement step.
alt: Subtractive replacement drops a dedicated etcd cluster to two voting members, while additive learner replacement keeps three healthy voting members throughout.
cap: Removing an etcd member before its replacement joins leaves no fault tolerance, so adding the new member as a learner first is the safer order.

name: k21-admission-chain
title: A request moves through admission before it reaches etcd
spec: A left-to-right row of checkpoint boxes, each joined by an arrow, with a request badge entering on the far left. Box 1, labelled Authentication and RBAC, with a shield icon: confirms the caller may perform the action. Box 2, labelled Mutating controllers, with a gear icon: built-in Service Account controller runs first and sets the default ServiceAccount, adds ImagePullSecrets and the token volume. Box 3, labelled Mutating webhooks, with a window icon: external services that return JSON patches. Box 4, labelled Schema validation, with a check icon: the object must match the defined schema, and it sees the finished object. Box 5, labelled Validating controllers and webhooks, with a lock icon: they admit or reject but cannot change the object, for example NamespaceLifecycle, ResourceQuota, and validating webhooks, which all must allow the request. Box 6, labelled etcd, with a disk cylinder icon, at the far right. Number circles 1 to 5 on the boxes (r=24, green, white numbers) show the order. Under box 5, an orange note: one rejection is enough to deny the request. Under box 2 and box 3, small grey labels: can change the object. Under box 5, grey label: can only admit or reject. Green takeaway bar: mutation runs before validation, so validation sees the final object, and the request stops at the first deny.
anchor: ### How a request moves through admission
alt: A request passes authentication and RBAC, then mutating controllers and webhooks, then schema validation, then validating checks, before it is stored in etcd.
cap: A request is changed by mutating checks first, then validated, and any single rejection stops it before it reaches etcd.

name: k21-csr-paths
title: Two kubelet certificate paths: auto-approved client, checked serving
spec: Top: a single start box labelled Kubelet with bootstrap token, joined by a line with arrowhead to a box labelled CertificateSigningRequest, with a form icon. The CSR then splits into two lanes. Lane A, labelled Client certificate, kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet: an arrow to a box labelled csrapproving in kube-controller-manager, marked Approved automatically, then an arrow to a box labelled Signer issues the client certificate, then a green end box labelled Node gets its client badge, with note: no human in the loop. Lane B, labelled Serving certificate, kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving: an arrow to a box labelled Checked by a person or approver, with a magnifier icon, labelled checks the SAN hostnames and IP addresses, then an arrow to a box labelled kubectl certificate approve or kubelet-csr-approver, then an arrow to an end box labelled Serving certificate issued. An orange note on lane B: not auto-approved, because the SAN values must be checked first. Under lane A, a small grey note: the node authenticates only as system:node. Green takeaway bar: client badges are auto-approved by pattern, serving certificates need their names checked.
alt: A kubelet bootstrap token leads to a CSR; client certificates are approved automatically, while serving certificates wait for a check of their names.
cap: Kubelet client certificates are approved automatically, but serving certificates wait for a check because their names must be correct.

name: k21-pod-identity-evolution
title: From node-wide keys to per-pod short-lived tokens
spec: Three columns drawn as stepped boxes, left to right, ordered from weakest to strongest, with an arrow between each column labelled fixes the problem before it. Column 1, titled kube2iam: a worker node box with a DaemonSet agent and an iptables redirect, pointing to the EC2 metadata API. A label: the node instance profile must assume every role any pod uses, so a container breakout compromises every role. Icon: an unlocked key. Column 2, titled kiam: a server-node box with a kiam server, a node DaemonSet agent, and a user pod with spec.nodeName set to a server node, with a dashed arrow that jumps past a scheduler box, labelled bypasses the scheduler. Orange highlight on the dashed arrow. Label: pods can reach the metadata endpoint and assume unauthorized roles. Column 3, titled IRSA: a pod box with a projected token file, labelled audience sts.amazonaws.com and expirationSeconds 86400. An arrow to an AWS STS box labelled sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. An arrow from IAM to a note labelled verifies the JWT against the cluster OIDC discovery and JWKS. Label: no metadata proxy and no shared key. A small webhook icon marked mutating webhook injects the token and the environment variables AWS_ROLE_ARN and AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE. Green takeaway bar: each pod gets its own short-lived token, and no node holds a shared key.
alt: kube2iam gives every node one powerful key, kiam can be bypassed with spec.nodeName, and IRSA gives each pod a short-lived token exchanged with STS.
cap: IRSA gives each pod its own short-lived token exchanged with AWS STS, which removes the shared node-level key that the older proxies relied on.

name: k21-spire-attestation
title: SPIRE attests the node first, then the workload
spec: Top to bottom, two stages with an arrow between them. Stage 1, titled Node attestation: a box labelled spire-server, the central signing authority and registration store, with an arrow down to a box labelled spire-agent, a DaemonSet on every node. A label on the arrow reads k8s_psat platform evidence. Output arrow from spire-agent labelled X.509-SVID for the node. A dashed box shows the node entry guest list with three selectors: cluster name, namespace spire, service account spire-agent, must all match. Stage 2, titled Workload attestation: a box labelled Workload, with a process icon, connected by a Unix domain socket arrow labelled unix:///run/spire/sockets/agent.sock to the spire-agent. A small note: no secret is carried by the workload. The spire-agent inspects the caller's pod namespace, service account, pod labels and container image, and matches them against the registration entries with parent ID spiffe://.../nodes. Output arrow from the agent labelled X.509-SVID or JWT-SVID for service-a. Number circles 1 and 2 on the two stages. Orange note on the matching step: a pod with the right name but the wrong image gets nothing. Green takeaway bar: the node proves what it is with platform evidence, and the workload proves what it is with its pod metadata.
alt: SPIRE attests the node with platform evidence first, then matches a workload's pod metadata through the node-local agent socket.
cap: SPIRE first checks each node with platform evidence, then matches each workload's pod metadata before issuing its identity.

name: k22-abstraction-spectrum
title: Four stages of developer abstraction, from raw kubectl to invisible Kubernetes
spec: A wide horizontal arrow across the top, pointing right, labelled from more Kubernetes exposed to less Kubernetes exposed. Under the arrow, four equal columns numbered with circles 1 to 4 (r=24, green, white numbers). Column 1, titled Stage 1 raw CLI and local UIs: a small terminal icon; list items kubectl, kubectx, kubens, Octant and Lens (monospace for kubectl, kubectx, kubens); a label: full flexibility, every developer needs RBAC and Kubernetes knowledge. Column 2, titled Stage 2 templating: a stack-of-layers icon; boxes Helm chart with Values.yaml, then Kustomize patches what the chart does not cover, a label: developers still apply native objects. Column 3, titled Stage 3 custom workload CRDs: a box icon; a short YAML card labelled PinterestService, 25 lines replacing more than 350 lines of native YAML; a window labelled break-glass view into Pods, PVCs and events drawn as a second door on the column. Column 4, titled Stage 4 invisible Kubernetes: a cloud icon; labels Cloud Foundry, Backstage, HashiCorp Waypoint, and a short file labelled build, deploy, release. Under column 4 a grey note: developers never see Kubernetes. Orange highlight on the break-glass door in column 3 with the note: keep the emergency door. Under the four columns, a row of two labels at the two ends: left, most flexibility and most developer knowledge needed; right, fastest onboarding and highest platform maintenance burden for custom GPU or RDMA features. Green takeaway bar: each step to the right trades flexibility for simplicity.
anchor: ### The `Team` custom resource operator pattern and the 4-stage spectrum of platform abstractions
alt: Four stages move from raw kubectl with full flexibility to invisible Kubernetes with the fastest onboarding.
cap: Developer abstractions run from raw kubectl with full flexibility to invisible Kubernetes, and each step to the right trades flexibility for simplicity.

name: k22-cohort-borrow
title: A Kueue cohort: owned quota, borrowing and reclaim by preemption
spec: A top box labelled Cohort, a shared pool, drawn as a large rounded container. Inside it, two ClusterQueue boxes side by side: ClusterQueue team-a with nominalQuota marked as its owned GPUs, and ClusterQueue team-b with its own nominalQuota. Each queue box shows a row of GPU slots (small squares). Team-a's queue has its slots filled with a team-a job and, in addition, three slots filled with borrowed slots from team-b's idle quota, outlined with a dashed border and labelled borrowed. Team-b's queue has idle slots shown as empty squares. Numbered steps in circles 1 to 3 along the bottom: 1 team-a borrows idle quota from the cohort, 2 team-b submits a job and asks for its own share back, 3 team-a's borrowed work is preempted and the borrowed slots return to team-b. An orange arrow marks step 3 as the preemption. Labels in the boxes: borrowingLimit caps how much a team may borrow, written as text beside team-a. Icons: a car-park or bay icon for the queue slots is optional. Green takeaway bar: a team's owned quota comes back when its owner needs it, so the borrower loses running work.
alt: Teams in one cohort borrow each other's idle GPU quota, and the borrower is preempted when the owner reclaims it.
cap: Teams in a Kueue cohort can borrow idle GPU quota from each other, and a borrower is preempted when the owner needs its share back.

name: k23-overprovision-preempt
title: Warm buffer nodes hidden by negative-priority pause pods
spec: Three stages drawn left to right, each a row of GPU node boxes with pods shown as small blocks. Stage 1, titled Steady state: a warm GPU node box holding a row of pause pods (grey blocks) labelled cluster-overprovisioner, value -10, reserving nearly all of the node. A label: pause pods consume no real resources. Stage 2, titled Traffic spike: a real production inference pod (green block, priority 0 or more) arrives, with an arrow into the same warm node. A numbered step 1 on the arrow: kube-scheduler preempts the pause pods, with a 0 s node wait. The pause pods are shown being pushed out in orange. Stage 3, titled Buffer rebuilt: the pause pods are now Pending (dashed grey outline), with an arrow from them to a Cluster Autoscaler box, which adds a new buffer node in the background, labelled a new node joins in the background. Number circles 1, 2, 3 on the three stages (r=24, green). Orange highlight on the pause pods preempted in stage 2. Under the stages, a small note: the real pod starts at once on the warm node, instead of waiting for a new node to boot. Green takeaway bar: pause pods hold a warm node so the next burst does not wait for a new one to boot.
alt: Low-priority pause pods hold a warm GPU node; a real pod preempts them and starts at once while the autoscaler rebuilds the buffer.
cap: Low-priority placeholder pods hold a warm node, so a real pod can preempt them and start at once while a new buffer node boots in the background.

name: k23-gang-atomic
title: Pod-by-pod scale-up versus all-or-nothing capacity for a gang
spec: Two horizontal lanes stacked, each showing a 16-node gang needing all of its nodes before training starts. Top lane, titled Reactive scale-up pod by pod: a row of 16 node slots, the first several filled with green boxes labelled worker pod waiting, and the rest empty and dashed. An orange note: the waiting pods hold the new nodes idle while the rest are still being provisioned. A label: the gang cannot start with only part of its nodes. A small clock icon with the label scale-up trickles in. Bottom lane, titled ProvisioningRequest with Kueue AdmissionCheck: a single arrow labelled 1 request capacity for all 16 pods at once, leading to a bar with 16 node slots all filled and marked reserved. Then an arrow labelled 2 workload admitted, leading to a row of 16 running worker pods (green). A label: all or none, the nodes are held for the job. Numbered circles 1 and 2 on the bottom lane (r=24, green). Icons: a gear for the autoscaler, a lock for reserved capacity. Green takeaway bar: book the whole crew before anyone gets into the boat.
alt: Pod-by-pod scale-up fills nodes slowly and leaves partial capacity idle, while a ProvisioningRequest reserves all nodes before the gang starts.
cap: A ProvisioningRequest reserves capacity for the whole gang at once, while pod-by-pod scale-up can leave some nodes idle until the rest arrive.

name: k23-scale-down-window
title: The scale-down stabilization window remembers the highest recent recommendation
spec: A horizontal timeline from left to right labelled time, with a shaded rolling window of 600 seconds drawn as a band spanning the most recent ten minutes at the current moment. Above the timeline, a step line labelled desired replicas, rising to a high level during a busy period on the left, then dropping briefly during a dip in traffic in the middle, then recovering. A dashed horizontal line within the band marked stabilized value, the highest recommendation in the last 600 s, which stays high through the brief dip. Only at the right, after a sustained quiet period, does the stabilized value step down, shown with an orange arrow and label sustained quiet period lets the count fall. Small markers along the timeline: a brief dip labelled short dip, a long quiet span labelled sustained quiet. Numbered circles 1 and 2 at the two drops. Green takeaway bar: a brief dip does not remove replicas, only a sustained quiet period does.
alt: A scale-down window keeps the highest recent recommendation, so a brief dip keeps replicas while a sustained quiet period lets the count fall.
cap: A scale-down stabilization window keeps the highest recent recommendation, so only a sustained quiet period lets replicas be removed.

name: k24-alert-routing
title: How Alertmanager turns many firing alerts into a few calls
spec: A left-to-right flow. On the far left, a column of small alert cards labelled from Prometheus rules: several pod alerts on gpu-node-04, one NodeNotReady alert for gpu-node-04, one planned-maintenance mute, and one Watchdog card. An arrow from the column into a large box labelled Alertmanager, drawn as a switchboard. Inside the box, three numbered steps stacked top to bottom, each a rounded label with a gear icon: step 1 Group by alertname, cluster and namespace; step 2 Inhibit: NodeNotReady suppresses the pod alerts on the same node, drawn with a dashed grey arrow crossing out the pod cards; step 3 Silence: a time-bounded mute for planned maintenance on node gpu-node-07. Number circles 1 to 3 (r=24, green). On the right, three routes leave the box: a route labelled symptom that users feel, leading to a red-bordered box labelled Page on-call; a route labelled cause or capacity warning, leading to a box labelled Ticket or chat; and a route labelled Watchdog every 5 minutes, leading to an external box labelled heartbeat receiver, with a note: a missing heartbeat means the pipeline is broken. Orange highlight on the Watchdog route with the note: silence is the alarm. Green takeaway bar: page on symptoms, ticket on causes, and let the monitor prove it is alive.
alt: Alertmanager groups, inhibits and silences firing alerts, then routes symptoms to a page, causes to a ticket, and a Watchdog heartbeat to an external receiver.
cap: Alertmanager groups and suppresses related alerts, then sends symptoms to a page and causes to a ticket.

name: k24-log-path
title: A log line's path from stdout to Loki
spec: A left-to-right pipeline with five stages. Stage 1, at the far left: a container box labelled app writes to stdout and stderr, with a window icon. An arrow labelled runtime saves output to a file box labelled /var/log/pods, with a disk icon. Stage 2: a node DaemonSet box labelled node agent, Fluent Bit or Alloy, one per node, with three stacked sub-steps numbered 1 to 3 inside: 1 tail the files and parse CRI format; 2 add Kubernetes metadata: namespace, pod, labels, node; 3 filter health checks and redact secrets or PII. An arrow labelled ships to Stage 3: a box labelled Loki, with a label card showing exactly four index labels: job, namespace, pod and container, and a note: everything else stays inside the log line. An arrow from Loki into a box labelled Grafana Explore for LogQL queries, with a small example query in monospace: {namespace=training} |= NCCL WARN. Beneath the pipeline, a second row labelled node-level logs with three small boxes: journald from kubelet and containerd, dmesg with Xid messages, and API server audit logs, each with an arrow into the same node agent or Loki. A separate small box labelled Kubernetes Events, marked with an orange note: export events, they expire after 1 hour. Orange highlight on the label card with the note: keep Loki labels low-cardinality. Green takeaway bar: logs leave the pod the moment they are written, because a deleted pod takes its files with it.
alt: Container output is written to node files, tailed by a per-node agent that adds metadata and filters lines, then stored in Loki with four low-cardinality labels.
cap: Container logs are tailed by a per-node agent, enriched with metadata, and stored in Loki under a few low-cardinality labels.

name: k24-trace-handoff
title: A trace stays connected across services through a header handoff
spec: Three service boxes left to right: Service A (gateway), Service B (payments), Service C (database). Above them, a horizontal timeline bar for each service, showing its span as a bar: the span listPayments in Service B sits inside the time range of the request span in Service A, and a child span SQL query sits inside Service B's span, nested. An arrow between Service A and Service B labelled HTTP request with traceparent header, and an arrow from B to C labelled span context injected into outgoing headers. Three numbered steps on the arrow into Service B: 1 extract the parent's identity from the incoming headers; 2 start a child span that belongs to that parent; 3 finish the span when the handler returns. Small monospace labels for tracer function names: Extract, StartSpan, Inject, Finish. An orange marker on the arrow into Service C with the note: a missing inject step breaks the trace at this boundary. Under the boxes, a legend: Trace is all the spans of one request; Span is one timed operation; Tag is metadata on a span. Icons: a route arrow for the trace, a clock for span timing. Green takeaway bar: pass the trace context along on every call, or the trace is cut in two.
alt: A request carries its trace context in headers from one service to the next, where each service extracts it, starts a child span, and injects it into the next call.
cap: Each service reads the trace context from incoming headers and passes it on, so one request stays a single connected trace.

name: k24-burn-windows
title: Multi-window burn-rate alerts: a long window confirms, a short window checks now
spec: A horizontal timeline from left to right labelled time, marked with an outage that begins at a point on the left and is fixed at a point on the right. Two shaded window bands drawn over the timeline at the moment of evaluation: a long band labelled 1 h window, confirms the budget really burned, and a short band labelled 5 min window, confirms the burn is still happening now. A horizontal threshold line across the chart labelled 14.4 times the 0.5 percent budget, which is the 7.2 percent error rate. Above the timeline, a step line for the error ratio: low before the outage, high during the outage, low after the fix. A green box labelled page fires only when both windows are above the threshold, at the centre. Orange highlight on the short window at the fix point, with the note: the 5 min window drops below the threshold within minutes, so the alert clears soon after a fix. Numbered circles 1 and 2 on the two windows (r=24, green). A small grey note on the long window: without it, a 30-second blip would page someone. Green takeaway bar: a page needs both a sustained burn and a current one.
alt: A burn-rate page fires only when both the one-hour and five-minute error ratios exceed 14.4 times the budget.
cap: A burn-rate page fires only when both the one-hour and five-minute windows are above the threshold, so a short blip stays quiet and a fixed outage clears quickly.

name: k25-capture-points
title: Where to capture packets on the path between two pods
spec: A left-to-right path across two node-sized panels. Left panel labelled Node A holds a client pod box with a window icon, labelled client pod, and a small pipe-shaped box labelled client veth attached to its edge. Right panel labelled Node B holds a server pod box with a window icon, labelled server pod, and a pipe-shaped box labelled server veth on its edge. Between the two panels a horizontal link labelled node uplink. A single arrow runs from the client pod through client veth, node uplink and server veth to the server pod, labelled packets. Three numbered capture markers, each a green circle r=24 with a white number, sit on the path: 1 at client veth, 2 at node uplink, 3 at server veth. Each marker has a short label under it with the source wording: capture here. Orange note under marker 2 and the node uplink: running tcpdump only on the node's primary interface misses the veth and bridge hops. Green takeaway bar: capture at each hop, so you see where the packets disappear.
alt: Packets from a client pod cross its veth, the node uplink and the server veth, and captures at each point show where they vanish.
cap: Capturing packets at the client veth, the node uplink and the server veth shows the hop where traffic disappears.

name: k25-nsenter-room
title: Host tools working inside a pod's network namespace
spec: Two stacked panels on a left-to-right layout. Top panel labelled Node (host): a box labelled host tools with small icons for tcpdump, ip, ss and curl, each icon with its name under it. A dashed green arrow labelled nsenter -t PID -n leads from host tools into a large rounded room on the right labelled pod network namespace. Inside the room a small box labelled pod app and a box labelled pod eth0. Bottom panel labelled Pod image: a small box labelled app image with the note: no tcpdump, ip or ss needed inside the image, drawn with a grey strike-through on those three names. Numbered steps inside the top panel: 1 find the PID with crictl inspect; 2 run host tools with nsenter -n. Orange note on the pod image panel: the host binaries stay under your control, not the app team's. Green takeaway bar: the room is the pod's network, and your tools come from the host.
alt: Host tools run through nsenter -n inside the pod's network namespace, so the pod image needs no debugging tools.
cap: The nsenter command runs the node's own tools inside a pod's network namespace, so the pod image needs none of them.

name: k25-oom-scope
title: Container limit versus node memory: two different OOM kills
spec: Two side-by-side panels titled by scope. Left panel titled Container limit: a dashed rounded box labelled memory limit (the cgroup ceiling) containing a filled green bar that reaches the top of the box, labelled container working set. Beside the box, a line labelled node memory: plenty free, drawn as a large light green block with white space. A label on the left panel: CONSTRAINT_MEMCG, the container hit its own ceiling, and an arrow labelled oom_kill pointing to a red-bordered box labelled container killed. Right panel titled Whole node: a large box labelled node memory with every container bar below its own dashed limit, and the bars together filling the node. A label: CONSTRAINT_NONE, the node ran short while every container stayed under its limit. Below it a red-bordered box labelled node-level kill. Under the right panel, a short fix row with three small boxes: reserve system memory; reduce workers; enforce Guaranteed QoS. Orange note on the left panel: a pod can be killed while the node still has free memory. Green takeaway bar: separate the container's limit from the node's use before you change anything.
alt: A container can hit its own memory limit while the node has memory free, and a node can run short while each container stays under its limit.
cap: A container OOM kill comes from its own memory limit, while a node-level kill means the whole host ran out of memory.

name: k26-pod-namespaces
title: Which namespaces a pod shares and which each container keeps
spec: One large rounded box labelled Pod. Inside it, at the top, a small box labelled pause container with a lock icon, and a wide green band spanning the full width of the pod labelled shared: net, ipc, uts, with the pause container drawn as the holder of that band. Below the band, two side-by-side container boxes, each with a window icon: left box labelled container 1, right box labelled container 2. Each container box has two private chips labelled mnt and pid. A small arrow from each container chip to the shared band labelled joins. Numbered notes, each a green circle r=24 with a white number: 1 the pause container creates the shared namespaces and holds them open; 2 each container gets its own mnt namespace; 3 each container usually gets its own pid namespace. Orange note on the pid chip: PID 1 ignores SIGTERM unless a handler is installed. Green takeaway bar: the pause container holds the shared view open while each container keeps its own filesystem view.
alt: A pod's containers share net, ipc and uts namespaces held open by the pause container, while each container keeps its own mnt and usually its own pid namespace.
cap: The pause container holds the net, ipc and uts namespaces open, so the containers in a pod share them while each keeps its own mount namespace.

name: k26-cpu-throttle-period
title: Eight threads drain a 2-CPU quota in 25 ms, then stall for 75 ms
spec: A horizontal timeline for one 100 ms CFS period, with tick marks at 0 ms, 25 ms, 50 ms, 75 ms and 100 ms on an axis labelled wall-clock time within one period. Label above the axis: cpu.max 200000 100000, a quota of 200 ms per 100 ms period. Eight thin horizontal lanes labelled thread 1 to thread 8, each with a green bar from 0 ms to 25 ms, so the lanes stack like parallel work. A counter box at the 25 ms point labelled quota used: 8 x 25 ms = 200 ms. From 25 ms to 100 ms a grey hatched band across all eight lanes labelled throttled 75 ms, all threads stalled. Numbered steps: 1 eight threads wake and run in parallel; 2 the quota is spent at 25 ms; 3 the cgroup stalls every thread for the remaining 75 ms. Orange note at the grey band: average CPU looks low, yet tail latency spikes and probes time out. Green takeaway bar: a limit counts CPU time across all threads, not cores at each instant.
alt: Eight parallel threads use the whole 200 ms quota in 25 ms of a 100 ms period, and the cgroup then stalls them for the remaining 75 ms.
cap: Eight threads on a 2-CPU limit spend the 200 ms quota in 25 ms, so the cgroup stalls them for the rest of the 100 ms period.

name: k26-overlay-copy-up
title: How overlayfs copies a whole file up before a write
spec: A left-to-right flow with a stacked-layers drawing on the left and steps on the right. Left: three stacked horizontal sheets. The bottom sheet, the largest, is labelled lowerdir, read-only image layers, with a disk icon. The middle sheet, labelled upperdir, writable container layer, sits above it. A thin sheet labelled workdir, scratch space sits beside them. On top of the stack, a merged box labelled container rootfs, the view the process sees. Right side, three numbered steps with number circles r=24: 1 a process opens an existing multi-GB file from lowerdir for writing; 2 overlayfs copies the entire file up into upperdir inside the open call; 3 only then can the first small write proceed. Orange note beside step 2: it is like photocopying a whole book before you underline one word. Dashed arrow from upperdir to the rootfs labelled the copy the process now writes to. Green takeaway bar: keep datasets and checkpoints on volumes, not in the container layer.
alt: A write to an image file in overlayfs first copies the whole file from the read-only lowerdir into the upperdir.
cap: Writing to an existing file in the image layer makes overlayfs copy the whole file up into the writable layer first.

name: k27-keyless-signing
title: Keyless signing: OIDC token, Fulcio certificate, Rekor log
spec: A left-to-right flow of four boxes joined by numbered arrows. Box 1 on the far left, labelled CI job (GitHub Actions workflow), with a gear icon. Box 2 labelled OIDC provider (token.actions.githubusercontent.com) with a lock icon. Box 3 labelled Fulcio, the certificate authority, with a certificate icon. Box 4 on the far right labelled Rekor, the transparency log, with a ledger icon. Arrow 1 from the CI job to the OIDC provider labelled short-lived OIDC token. Arrow 2 from the CI job to Fulcio labelled public key plus token, returning a short-lived certificate bound to the workflow identity, valid about 10 minutes. Arrow 3 from the CI job to Rekor labelled signature and certificate recorded. Number circles r=24 green with white numbers 1, 2, 3 on the arrows. Under the CI job a small box labelled cosign signs the image digest with an ephemeral key, which is discarded after signing. Orange note on the discard box: no long-lived signing key exists to steal. No takeaway bar.
alt: A CI job gets a short-lived OIDC token, Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate for it, and the signature is recorded in the Rekor transparency log.
cap: Keyless signing uses a short-lived OIDC token and a Fulcio certificate, and records the signature in the Rekor log.

name: k27-admission-two-checks
title: Admission checks who built the image and where it came from
spec: Left-to-right flow. On the far left, a box labelled Pod create request with a window icon. An arrow into a large box labelled Admission (Kyverno verifyImages) with a shield icon. From the admission box two parallel arrows lead to two check panels stacked vertically. Top panel, numbered 1 with a green number circle r=24, titled Who built it: a signature and provenance from the GitHub workflow identity, with the note for Pods in production namespaces. Bottom panel, numbered 2, titled Where it came from: image from registry.example.com or nvcr.io, with the note for every Pod. Both panels have arrows going right into a decision box labelled Both pass? Yes arrow leads to a green box labelled Pod is admitted. No arrow leads to a red-bordered box labelled Pod is rejected. Orange note beside the two panels: a policy that answers only one of these questions leaves a gap. No takeaway bar.
alt: Admission checks the signature and provenance of the builder identity for production Pods, and checks that every image comes from an approved registry.
cap: Admission enforcement asks who built each image and where it came from, and rejects the Pod unless both checks pass.

name: k27-pickle-vs-safetensors
title: Why a pickle checkpoint runs code on load and safetensors does not
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel titled pickle (.pt, .bin, .pkl): a stack of small blocks showing a serialized object stream, with one block labelled __reduce__ naming an arbitrary callable, and a red arrow from that block to a box labelled code runs at torch.load. Under it a small note: the instant torch.load unpickles the file. Right panel titled safetensors (model.safetensors): two stacked blocks, the top labelled JSON header with the entries tensor names, dtypes, shapes and byte offsets, the bottom labelled raw flat tensor bytes. A green arrow from the file to a box labelled weights mapped straight to memory, zero copy. Under the right panel a note: runs no code. Between the two panels a middle row labelled weights_only=True, which restricts the unpickler to tensor data. Numbered steps with green number circles r=24: 1 the file is read; 2 the loader decides what runs; 3 the weights load. Orange note on the left panel: loading a pickle is the same as running a program you have not read. Green takeaway bar: a model file is code in disguise, so prefer safetensors.
alt: A pickle checkpoint can run code the moment torch.load reads it, while safetensors stores a JSON header and raw tensor bytes and runs no code.
cap: A pickle checkpoint can run code when torch.load reads it, while a safetensors file holds only a header and raw tensor bytes.

name: k28-envoy-route-path
title: How Envoy moves one request from listener to endpoint
spec: A left-to-right chain of four boxes, each with a number circle r=24 green with a white number: 1, 2, 3, 4. Box 1 labelled listener, with a door icon, note binds a port such as 80 and 443, the front door. Box 2 labelled filter chain, with a gear icon, note HTTP connection manager, the sorting step. Box 3 labelled route, with a signpost icon, note matches by path or header. Box 4 labelled cluster, with a delivery van icon, note the group of endpoints for one service. From box 4 an arrow to a final small box labelled endpoints. Above the chain, four smaller discovery boxes, each connected by a dashed arrow down to its stage: LDS feeds listener, RDS feeds route, CDS feeds cluster, EDS feeds endpoints. Under the endpoints box a small label: attached through a ClusterLoadAssignment. Orange note on the endpoints link: Envoy has no Endpoint object in the EDS API. Green takeaway bar: listeners accept, filters decide, and clusters receive the traffic.
alt: Envoy sends a request from a listener through a filter chain and a route to a cluster, whose endpoints come from EDS.
cap: Envoy handles a request in four steps, from listener to filter chain, route and cluster, with the xDS APIs feeding each stage.

name: k28-retry-doubling
title: A retry doubles the load on a slow model server
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel titled Every caller retries once: a client icon sends a request to a model server box labelled vllm, which is slow. A second arrow from the client labelled retry sends the same request again to the same server. A load gauge under the server reads 2x load, drawn as two full bars against a one-bar reference line. Orange note: the load doubles at the exact moment the server can least afford more. Right panel titled Generation POST with retries.attempts: 0: the same client sends one request to the vllm box, with no retry arrow. The gauge reads 1x load, one bar. Under the right panel, two smaller labelled boxes: retryOn: connect-failure,refused-stream for idempotent calls such as embeddings and health checks. Numbered steps with green circles r=24: 1 a slow server; 2 a retry is added; 3 the server takes twice the load. Green takeaway bar: retries multiply load, so set attempts to 0 for generation requests.
alt: When every caller retries a slow model server once, the server load doubles, while setting retries to zero for generation requests keeps load at one.
cap: Retrying a slow model server doubles its load, so generation requests should not be retried.

name: k28-native-sidecar-order
title: Sidecar start and stop order: regular container versus native sidecar
spec: Two horizontal lanes on one shared time axis labelled pod lifecycle, from start to end. Top lane titled Sidecar as a regular container: a bar for the app container and a bar for the proxy container that start together. A red-bordered marker where the app makes an early call before the proxy is ready, labelled connection refused. At the end, the app bar stops when the job finishes, but the proxy bar keeps running, with a label: the Job never completes. Bottom lane titled Native sidecar (initContainers with restartPolicy: Always): the proxy bar starts first in the init phase, a small marker labelled startupProbe waits for proxy ready, then the app bar starts. At the end the proxy bar stops after all main containers exit. Numbered green circles r=24 on the bottom lane: 1 proxy starts first; 2 app starts once the proxy is ready; 3 proxy stops after the main containers exit. Orange note on the top lane's still-running proxy: the pod stays alive, so the Job never completes. No takeaway bar.
alt: A regular sidecar starts with the app and keeps a finished Job alive, while a native sidecar starts first and stops after the main containers exit.
cap: A native sidecar starts before the app and stops after the main containers exit, which fixes the startup race and the stuck Job.

name: k29-webapp-fanout
title: One short WebApp object becomes six Kubernetes resources
spec: A left-to-right fan-out. On the far left, a small document card labelled WebApp (webapp-sample), the short request, with a note: one short object. An arrow from the card into a box labelled WebApp Operator, drawn as a gear with a watch-eye icon, with the note: watches for WebApp resources. From the operator a set of six arrows fan out to six child boxes stacked in a column on the right, each with a simple outline icon and a title and a short role line: Deployment (stateless front end); StatefulSet (relational database); ConfigMap (front end config file); Secret (credentials for the database); Service (routes traffic to the Deployment's backend Pods); Ingress (routing rules). Group the six child boxes inside one large green container labelled the long answer the operator writes. Orange highlight on the WebApp card with the note: the short request. Green takeaway bar: someone writes one short object, and the operator does the rest.
anchor: ### Kinds, resources and a WebApp example
alt: A short WebApp object is watched by the operator, which creates a Deployment, StatefulSet, ConfigMap, Secret, Service and Ingress.
cap: A WebApp operator turns one short WebApp object into six child resources that together run the app.

name: k29-owner-vs-finalizer
title: Owner references clean up children, finalizers clean up outside the cluster
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel titled ownerReferences: in-cluster children. A CR box labelled GPUHealthPolicy being deleted, with an arrow labelled deleted into a garbage collector box. From the garbage collector, arrows to three child boxes labelled Deployment, Service and ConfigMap, each with a dashed strike-through, labelled removed automatically. A label under the panel: works even if the operator Pod is down. Right panel titled finalizers: external cleanup. A CR box with a marker labelled deletionTimestamp set and finalizer platform.example.com/cleanup present. Numbered steps with green number circles r=24: 1 the operator sees the deletion mark; 2 it cleans up the outside work, shown as small boxes labelled cordoned nodes, cloud bucket, DNS record; 3 it removes the finalizer, and the object disappears. Orange note under the right panel: the uninstall trap: if the operator is deleted first, nobody removes the finalizer, and the CR stays in Terminating. Green takeaway bar: delete CRs before you uninstall their operator.
anchor: ### Garbage collection, owner references and finalizers
alt: Owner references let the garbage collector delete in-cluster children, while a finalizer makes the operator clean up external resources before the object is removed.
cap: Owner references let the garbage collector remove in-cluster children, while finalizers hold deletion until the operator cleans up outside work.

name: k29-schema-gate
title: The API server checks a custom resource before any controller sees it
spec: A left-to-right flow. On the far left, a box labelled Apply manifest with a document icon. An arrow into a large box labelled API server schema check, drawn as a gate, with three stacked checks inside, each a rounded label with a numbered green circle r=24: 1 enum: deploymentTier must be dev, stg or prod; 2 default: webAppReplicas defaults to 2 when omitted; 3 pruning: undeclared fields are dropped. From the gate two outcome paths. Upper path, for the manifest with deploymentTier qa: a red-bordered box labelled Refused, nothing stored, with a note: the operator never hears about the request. Lower path, for a manifest that leaves out webAppReplicas: an arrow labelled stored in etcd with replicas set to 2, leading to a box labelled Operator sees a complete object. Orange note on the Refused box: the schema did its job before any controller ran. Green takeaway bar: a good schema removes work from the controller.
alt: The API server checks the enum, fills in defaults and prunes unknown fields before it stores a custom resource, and it refuses an invalid value outright.
cap: The API server checks each custom resource against the schema, refusing invalid values and filling in defaults before any operator runs.

name: k30-change-three-ways
title: Three ways to change a node without overwriting someone else
spec: Three side-by-side panels, each a short flow, titled from left to right. Panel 1 titled Get and Update: a box labelled Get node reads the object, a box labelled edit label, then a box labelled Update. A red-bordered arrow from another actor labelled another controller writes first leads to the Update step, and a red box labelled 409 Conflict. Under it: fragile, a stale copy fails. Panel 2 titled RetryOnConflict: the same three boxes inside a loop arrow labelled retry, with a note: read again on each attempt, then Update succeeds. Panel 3 titled Patch or apply: a single box labelled send only the changed field, with a merge patch body shown as a small box labelled labels only, and one arrow to a box labelled node updated, with the note: one round trip, no read first. Numbered green circles r=24 in Panel 3: 1 send only the changed field; 2 the server applies it. Orange note on Panel 1's conflict box: a full Update from a stale copy can silently undo another writer's change. Green takeaway bar: prefer patch or apply over get-modify-update.
alt: A full Update from a stale copy can conflict, retrying re-reads and succeeds, and a merge patch changes only the field it names.
cap: A plain Update from a stale copy can fail with a conflict, while a patch sends only the field it changes.

name: k30-bounded-probes
title: Fan out probes with a 16-slot gate and one results channel
spec: A left-to-right fan-out. On the far left, a box labelled nodes (a list of node names). Arrows fan out to a column of goroutine boxes, drawn as stacked small cards labelled probe goroutine, several shown with a dotted tail to indicate more. Between the nodes and the probes, a vertical gate box labelled sem, 16 slots, drawn as a turnstile with sixteen small squares, each a slot; a probe must take a slot before it runs and gives it back when done. From the probes an arrow into a channel box labelled results channel, with a note: the probe sends unless ctx is done. From the results channel an arrow to a box labelled out map, filled by the loop that reads until the channel closes. Beside the probes a box labelled WaitGroup, with a note: a separate goroutine closes results after every probe finishes. Numbered green circles r=24: 1 take a slot in sem; 2 run the probe; 3 send the result or stop on ctx.Done; 4 close results when all are done. A 30-second timeout box at the top labelled context WithTimeout 30s. Orange note on the sem gate: at most 16 probes run at once. Green takeaway bar: every goroutine needs a clear way to exit, or it leaks.
alt: Probe goroutines take one of 16 semaphore slots, send results on a channel, and the channel closes after the WaitGroup finishes.
cap: The prober runs node checks in goroutines limited to 16 at a time, sends results on a channel, and closes it when all probes finish.

name: k30-error-wrap-chain
title: Wrapping an API error with %w and unwrapping it with errors.Is
spec: A top-to-bottom chain of three layered boxes stacked like nested envelopes on the left, and the caller on the right. Innermost box labelled API error: NotFound, the raw error from the API server, with a small icon of a magnifier. Middle box labelled wrapped with %w, cordon <node name>: ErrNoSuchNode, with a link icon. Outer box labelled returned to caller, the error value that the function returns. Between each layer a short arrow labelled wraps. On the right, the caller box with two check cards with arrows pointing back into the chain: a card labelled errors.Is ErrNoSuchNode, which follows the chain down to the named error; a card labelled errors.As, with the note: pulls a typed error out of the chain. Numbered green circles r=24 on the wraps: 1 the API call fails; 2 the function wraps it with %w; 3 the caller unwraps with errors.Is or errors.As. Orange note on a plain %v: it prints the message but drops the link to the original error. Green takeaway bar: wrap each error with %w so the caller can still reach the cause.
alt: A Go error wrapped with %w keeps the original API error reachable, so errors.Is and errors.As can find it from the caller.
cap: Wrapping an error with %w keeps the original cause reachable, so the caller can test it with errors.Is or errors.As.

name: k31-reconcile-steps
title: One Reconcile pass: observe, decide, act, report
spec: A horizontal flow of four rounded boxes left to right, each with a numbered circle (1 to 4, r=24, green, white number) and an icon. Box 1, icon clipboard or eye, title Observe, with a small monospace line below it reading r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, &policy) and a second line reading list nodes. Box 2, icon scales or decision diamond, title Decide, with the line Plan(verdicts, budget) below it, and a note that this step is a pure function with no I/O. Box 3, icon gear, title Act, with the line cordon each node in the plan below it. Box 4, icon document, title Report, with the line updateStatus below it. Arrows run 1 to 2, 2 to 3 and 3 to 4 as plain horizontal arrows. Above box 1 sits a small input box labelled req ctrl.Request with the note carries only namespace and name, linked by one arrow down into Observe. Below the flow sits a branch row with the four return options as small labelled chips reading Result{}, nil for done, Result{}, err for failure with backoff, Result{RequeueAfter: d}, nil for a timed re-check, and Result{Requeue: true}, nil for an immediate requeue, each drawn with no arrows and grouped under a label Return value tells the queue what happens next. Orange highlight on the Report box with the note write the status only when it changed. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reading the request holds only a name, so every pass re-reads the world.
alt: A Reconcile pass runs four steps in order: observe the policy and nodes, decide with a pure function, act on the plan, and report status.
cap: One Reconcile pass observes the cluster, decides with a pure function, acts, and reports, and the return value tells the queue what happens next.

name: k31-event-filter
title: From a watch event to a queued key
spec: A left-to-right layout with three event sources stacked on the left column inside one light green container labelled Watched objects. Source 1 box labelled For(&Policy{}) with the note your own resource. Source 2 box labelled Owns(&Child{}) with the note objects you created and own. Source 3 box labelled Watches(&Node{}, handler.EnqueueRequestsFromMapFunc(fn)) with the note objects you do not own. Each source has one arrow pointing right into a filter column. The filter column is a vertical stack of two predicate boxes inside a container labelled Predicates, each with a small funnel icon: box one labelled GenerationChangedPredicate with the note skips status-only updates of the primary, box two labelled custom Node predicate with the note drops heartbeat-only updates. Orange highlight on the custom Node predicate box. A dashed no path from the predicate column down to a grey box labelled dropped event, meaning no reconcile runs. A yes arrow continues right from the predicates to a box labelled mapping function fn that turns the object into requests, here the source 2 event goes straight through with the note owner lookup. Then one arrow into a box labelled work queue holding reconcile.Request keys, with the note namespace and name only. Then one arrow into a final box labelled Reconcile(ctx, req) with the note re-reads the object from the cache. Under the flow, one monospace line reads mgr.GetFieldIndexer().IndexField registered before the manager starts, linked by a dotted line to the Reconcile box as a note that List calls with client.MatchingFields use the index. Green takeaway bar: predicates decide what wakes the reconciler, and the queue holds only keys.
alt: Watch events pass through predicates that drop noise, then a mapping step turns each event into a queued namespace and name key for Reconcile.
cap: Watch events pass through predicates that drop noise, and only the surviving events reach the work queue as namespace and name keys.

name: k31-finalizer-flow
title: A finalizer holds deletion until cleanup runs
spec: A horizontal timeline from left to right with five numbered steps (number circles r=24, green). Step 1, box titled Add finalizer, with the monospace line controllerutil.AddFinalizer then r.Update, and the note before any side effect. Step 2, box titled Side effects, with the note cordon nodes the policy owns. Step 3, a branch box titled User deletes the policy, with a note that the API server sets a deletion timestamp and keeps the object visible. Step 4, box titled Release all, with the note undo every cordon the policy made, and an orange loop arrow curving back from a outlined sub-box labelled release failed, retry with the note returns the error so the queue retries. Step 5, box titled Remove finalizer, with the monospace line controllerutil.RemoveFinalizer then r.Update, and an arrow into a final grey box labelled object deleted by the API server. Above steps 1 and 2 a bracket labelled normal life, above steps 3 to 5 a bracket labelled deletion path. A side note box with a warning icon reads never leave a finalizer that nothing will remove, and a monospace line kubectl patch ... finalizers=null as the documented escape hatch. Green takeaway bar: the finalizer is armed before the side effect, so cleanup cannot be skipped.
alt: A finalizer is added before side effects, holds the object during deletion while cleanup runs, and is removed only after cleanup succeeds.
cap: A finalizer is added before any side effect and holds the object in place during deletion until the controller finishes cleanup and removes it.

name: k32-decision-pipeline
title: Judge, Budget and Plan: from node verdicts to the nodes to act on
spec: A left-to-right pipeline of four stages. Stage 1 on the far left is a stack of three small node cards labelled node A, node B and node C, inside a light green container labelled matched nodes. Each card has a short monospace line: node A with the note Unhealthy, node B with the note Pending and a WaitFor value, and node C with the note Healthy. An arrow from the container goes into Stage 2 box titled Judge(p, n, now) with the one-line note one pure verdict per node, no I/O. Stage 2 emits an arrow into Stage 3 box titled Budget(maxUnavailable, matched) with a small monospace note maxUnavailableNodes to a count, and beside it a note invalid or negative gives 0, missing gives all matched. Stage 3 emits an arrow into Stage 4 box titled Plan(verdicts, budget), drawn larger. Inside Plan, show a room calculation strip: budget minus already unschedulable nodes equals room, shown as a monospace line room = budget - unavailable. Below Plan, two outputs: a green box labelled act with the note candidates sorted by name, filled into the room, and an outlined box labelled blocked with the note extra candidates wait, BudgetExhausted event. Human maintenance cordons appear as a small grey chip labelled already unschedulable, with an arrow into the room calculation, labelled counts against the budget. Orange highlight on the blocked output with the note nothing is taken past the budget. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Judge decides each node alone, Budget sets the ceiling, and Plan fills the room in name order.
alt: Judge classifies each node, Budget turns the budget into a count, and Plan fills the room left after unschedulable nodes, sending the rest to blocked.
cap: Judge classifies each node, Budget turns the budget into a count, and Plan acts on candidates only within the room left after unschedulable nodes.

name: k32-window-timeline
title: Waiting for a window without sleeping
spec: A horizontal timeline from left to right along one axis labelled time. Three marked points on the axis. Point T0 labelled condition turns False, with a note LastTransitionTime is set. A shaded span from T0 to T0 plus 2m labelled unhealthyFor (2m) with the note Judge returns Pending and WaitFor. At the end of that span a point labelled T0 plus 2m, with the note Judge returns Unhealthy, the node is cordoned, and an arrow up from it to a small box labelled cordon patch with the three annotations platform.example.com/cordoned-by, platform.example.com/cordon-reason and platform.example.com/cordoned-at. Between T0 and T0 plus 2m, a curved dashed arrow from the timeline back to a box labelled Reconcile returns RequeueAfter, with the note the queue wakes the reconciler at the exact moment the window ends, and no sleep runs inside Reconcile. Later point T1 labelled condition turns True, with a shaded span from T1 to T1 plus 5m labelled healthyFor (5m) with the note Judge returns HealthyWaitFor until the span ends. At the end of that span a point labelled T1 plus 5m, with a note Judge returns Healthy, and the owned node is uncordoned. Number circles (r=24, green) at points 1 to 4 marking the order: 1 at T0, 2 at the requeue, 3 at T0 plus 2m, 4 at the uncordon. Orange highlight on the cordon step. A small note under the healthy span reads a flapping condition restarts the healthy window, as the chapter describes the healthy window as the hysteresis that stops flapping. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: the operator holds no timers, it asks the queue to call it back when the window ends.
alt: A node cordons only after its unhealthy window passes, and the reconciler asks to be called back at that moment instead of sleeping.
cap: The reconciler waits for a window by asking the queue to call it back at the exact moment the window ends, so it never sleeps.

name: k32-provenance-release
title: Only the policy's own cordons are released
spec: Two-part layout. Left part: a light green container labelled Nodes in the cluster with three node boxes in a row. Node gpu-01 shows a small person icon and a grey tag labelled no owner annotation, with the status line unschedulable true, and the note a human cordon. Node gpu-02 shows a tag labelled platform.example.com/cordoned-by: h100-pool and the status line unschedulable true. Right part: a vertical flow of three numbered steps with number circles r=24. Step 1 box labelled kubectl cordon gpu-01 with the note a human SRE cordons the node. Step 2 box labelled gpu-02 turns unhealthy with the note the policy h100-pool cordons it and writes its owner annotation. Step 3 box labelled kubectl delete gpuhealthpolicy h100-pool with the note the finalizer runs releaseAll. Below step 3, a decision diamond labelled cordoned-by equals h100-pool? with two arrows: yes goes to a green box labelled uncordon gpu-02, and no goes to a grey box labelled leave gpu-01 cordoned. Orange highlight on the no branch with the note the human cordon is never touched. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: the owner annotation is the proof of which cordon is ours.
alt: On policy deletion, the operator uncordons only the nodes whose owner annotation names it, and leaves a human cordon in place.
cap: When the policy is deleted, only nodes carrying its own owner annotation are uncordoned, and a human cordon stays in place.

name: k33-node-operand-gating
title: Node labels decide which operand DaemonSets land on a node
spec: Left-to-right layout. On the far left, a node box titled GPU node with a small chip icon, containing three label chips stacked vertically: nvidia.com/gpu.present=true at the top, then nvidia.com/gpu.workload.config with the value container, then nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.operands=false drawn as a grey chip with a note that it switches all operands off. Add a fourth optional chip nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.dcgm-exporter=false, drawn grey with the note disables only that operand. An arrow from the node box goes right into a column labelled gpuStateLabels table in state_manager.go. Inside the column two rows. Row one, labelled container, lists the matching deploy labels as a monospace chip reading driver, container-toolkit, device-plugin, dcgm, dcgm-exporter, gpu-feature-discovery and operator-validator, each set to true. Row two, labelled vm-passthrough, lists sandbox-validator, vfio-manager and sandbox-device-plugin set to true, and the container labels set to false. Each row has an arrow into a column of DaemonSet boxes on the right, one per operand, labelled driver DaemonSet, container toolkit DaemonSet, device plugin DaemonSet and dcgm-exporter DaemonSet, each with the note selected by its nodeSelector. Only the container row arrows reach these DaemonSets, drawn in green. The vm-passthrough row points to a separate box labelled VFIO and sandbox plugin pods, drawn with a dashed border. Orange highlight on the operands=false chip with the note removes every GPU Operator pod from that node. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: a DaemonSet runs only where its nodeSelector label matches, like a name tag on a door.
anchor: ## 5. Node gating and the validator chain
alt: A node's workload config and deploy labels select which operand DaemonSets run on it, and an operands false label removes them all.
cap: A node's deploy labels decide which operand DaemonSets run there, so a container node and a passthrough node get different sets of pods.

name: k33-upgrade-states
title: A driver upgrade moves one node through labelled states
spec: A vertical state chain on the left half of the figure, drawn top to bottom, with each state a rounded box containing its label in monospace. The top box is titled nvidia.com/gpu-driver-upgrade-state above the chain. States in order, each linked to the next by a down arrow: upgrade-required (note: driver pod revision hash differs from the target DaemonSet revision), cordon-required (note: node is cordoned), wait-for-jobs (note: waits for running GPU jobs, up to a timeout), pod-deletion or drain (note: GPU pods evicted and operator pods holding /dev/nvidia* stopped), pod-restart (note: OnDelete driver pod is deleted so the new one starts), validation (note: validator pod must pass on the new driver), uncordon. From uncordon, two branches: an arrow to done, drawn green, and a dashed arrow from validation to failed in grey. Number circles r=24 at the steps 1 to 7 along the chain. On the right side, a side box titled Limits with the note a maximum number of parallel upgrades and an unavailability budget, linked by a thin line to the top of the chain. Orange highlight on the pod-restart box with the note the OnDelete strategy means the operator, not the DaemonSet controller, restarts the driver. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: each node holds one label that tells you exactly where its upgrade is stuck.
anchor: ## 6. Drivers: DaemonSet vs NVIDIADriver CRD, and upgrades
alt: A driver upgrade moves each node through a fixed series of labelled states, from upgrade-required through validation to done or failed.
cap: Each node moves through a fixed series of upgrade labels, so reading the label tells you where a stuck driver upgrade has stopped.

name: k33-wait-compare
title: Two ways a node can make later operands wait
spec: A two-column comparison with a header row. Left column titled GPU Operator: validator files and init containers. Right column titled Network Operator: mofed.wait label and nodeSelector. Each column has the same three stacked rows. Row 1 titled Who waits: left shows the downstream pod, drawn as a box inside the node, with the note it waits inside the node in an init loop; right shows the scheduler, drawn outside the node, with the note it simply does not place the pod. Row 2 titled The signal: left shows a file under /run/nvidia/validations, for example driver-ready and toolkit-ready, written by the validator; right shows a node label network.nvidia.com/operator.mofed.wait, set to true while the OFED pod is not ready and flipped to false once it is ready. Row 3 titled What you see with kubectl get pods: left shows the pod in Init:0/1 right on the node; right shows no pod on the node until the label flips to false. Between the columns, a thin vertical divider with a small label both solve the same per-node dependency problem. Orange highlight on the right column row 3 with the note the pod does not appear at all. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: one waits at the node, the other waits at the scheduler, and both wait for the driver on the same node.
anchor: ### Wait labels: dependency ordering without the controller waiting
alt: The GPU Operator makes pods wait inside the node using marker files, while the Network Operator makes pods wait at the scheduler using a node label.
cap: The GPU Operator makes downstream pods wait inside the node using marker files, while the Network Operator keeps them off the node with a label.

name: k34-pool-after-create
title: What a GPU node pool sets up after creation
spec: A top-to-bottom sequence of four numbered steps, each a rounded box with a number circle (r=24, green, white number) and a small icon, joined by down arrows. Step 1 box titled Node pool created with the monospace line gcloud container node-pools create h100-pool and the note accelerator type=nvidia-h100-80gb,count=8. Step 2 box titled GPU driver DaemonSet with the note GKE installs it when gpu-driver-version is not disabled, drawn as a small stack of three identical pod icons, one per GPU node. Step 3 box titled Node advertises nvidia.com/gpu with the note through the GKE device plugin, and beside it a label chip cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator=nvidia-h100-80gb and a taint chip nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule drawn in grey. Step 4 box titled Pod requests a GPU with the monospace line resources.limits nvidia.com/gpu: 8 and the note the admission step adds a matching toleration automatically. An arrow from the taint chip at step 3 to step 4 labelled matched by an automatic toleration. Orange highlight on the taint chip with the note a CPU-only Pod without the toleration is kept off this node. Side note under step 2, drawn as a dashed box: set gpu-driver-version=disabled only if the GPU Operator installs the driver, and never let both install drivers on one node. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: the pool creates the driver, the advertised GPU count, the label and the taint in one step.
alt: After a GPU node pool is created, GKE installs the driver, advertises nvidia.com/gpu, labels and taints the nodes, and admits only GPU Pods with the matching toleration.
cap: After a GPU node pool is created, GKE installs the driver, advertises the GPU resource, and taints the nodes so that only GPU Pods land there.

name: k34-sharing-walls
title: Three ways to share a GPU, from shared desk to separate offices
spec: Three panels side by side, left to right, each titled with its technique name, arranged by increasing walls. Left panel titled Time-sharing with a single GPU drawn as a box, two small container boxes labelled container A and container B taking turns, drawn with a clock icon and arrows showing alternating time slots. Under it a label Shared desk, memory and faults are shared, with an orange warning chip reading no fault isolation. Middle panel titled MPS with one GPU box and several process boxes working at the same time, joined to the GPU by parallel arrows, with a dashed wall partially between them, labelled shared room, and a note shares fault fate. Right panel titled MIG with one GPU box split into three separate partitions, each with its own dedicated memory block and its own compute block, separated by solid walls, labelled separate offices, and a green note dedicated memory and compute per partition. Under the three panels a horizontal arrow from left to right labelled more walls means stronger isolation and fewer workloads per card. Orange highlight on the time-sharing warning chip with the note never use it for tenants you do not trust. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: each step to the right adds walls, and each wall costs some density.
anchor: ## 7. Sharing a GPU: time-sharing, MPS, MIG
alt: Time-sharing, MPS and MIG share one GPU with increasing walls, from turn-taking containers to hardware partitions with dedicated memory.
cap: Time-sharing, MPS and MIG share one GPU with more isolation at each step, and stronger isolation fits fewer workloads per card.

name: k34-spot-window
title: A Spot preemption gives about 25 to 30 seconds to save
spec: A horizontal timeline from left to right with three marked points on an axis labelled time. Point T0 labelled preemption notice, with a note the provider sends the signal and kubelet sends SIGTERM to the Pods. A shaded span from T0 to T0 plus 25 to 30 seconds labelled grace period (verify), drawn in a wide light green band. Inside the span, a sub-bar labelled checkpoint write, drawn as a bar that ends too late, with an orange dashed outline and the note a checkpoint written at the end of a long step may not finish in time. Point T1 at the end of the span labelled VM hard-terminated. Above the timeline, a row of three number circles r=24 green: 1 at T0, 2 at the start of the checkpoint bar, 3 at T1. Below the timeline, two boxes side by side. Left box titled Option 1 with the note stateless or idempotent work, such as batch scoring or inference behind a load balancer. Right box titled Option 2 with the note frequent asynchronous checkpointing, paired with elastic torchrun or JobSet restart. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: checkpoint often enough that a notice this short still leaves something to resume from.
alt: A Spot preemption gives a short grace period, so a checkpoint must be frequent enough to finish before the VM is terminated.
cap: A Spot preemption gives only about 25 to 30 seconds of notice, so a checkpoint has to be frequent enough to save progress in that window.

name: k34-gpu-nics
title: Where GPU traffic goes on a multi-node training node
spec: A layout drawing of one accelerator VM box in the centre, labelled GPU node, containing a row of eight small GPU chips labelled GPU 1 to GPU 8, joined by a band labelled NVLink and NVSwitch inside the box. On the right edge of the VM box, two arrows leave: one thin grey arrow labelled default VPC network, and a set of thick green arrows labelled GPU NICs with the note dedicated to GPU traffic. The GPU NIC arrows lead to a box on the far right labelled fabric to other nodes, with the note compact placement keeps nodes close. Above the VM box, a row of three small config chips: gVNIC with the flag --enable-gvnic, multi-networking with the flag --enable-multi-networking and --additional-node-network, and NCCL plugin with the note TCPXO or RoCE RDMA depending on the machine generation. Below the fabric box, a small chip labelled compact placement with the flag --placement-type COMPACT. Orange highlight on the GPU NIC arrows with the note these carry the gradient traffic between nodes. A small box at the bottom reads validate with all_reduce_perf before a long run. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: GPU traffic gets its own NICs, so it does not compete with ordinary network traffic.
alt: A multi-node GPU VM sends GPU traffic over dedicated GPU NICs to the fabric, while ordinary traffic uses the default VPC network.
cap: A multi-node GPU VM sends gradient traffic over dedicated GPU NICs, so it does not compete with ordinary network traffic.

name: k35-geodns-anycast
title: GeoDNS hands out a regional address, anycast shares one address everywhere
spec: A two-panel comparison, left and right, with a header row. Left panel titled GeoDNS. At the top a user box labelled user with a phone icon, an arrow down to a box labelled recursive DNS resolver (ISP cache), then an arrow down to a box labelled DNS answer: regional cluster IP. From the DNS answer, three arrows fan out to three regional cluster boxes labelled cluster US, cluster EU and cluster Asia, with one cluster box drawn with a dashed grey outline and the note removed from DNS but still cached. A small note box beside the resolver reads caches may ignore the short TTL and keep old answers, and another note reads the location seen is the resolver, not the user. Right panel titled Anycast. One virtual address box labelled one global IP advertised with BGP at the top, with three edge location boxes labelled edge location A, edge location B and edge location C beneath it, each with an arrow from the same address. A single user box at the bottom left with one arrow to the nearest edge location, drawn as a solid green arrow. A note reads routing picks the closest by network performance, and another reads the balancer health-checks clusters and routes each HTTP request to a healthy one. Orange highlight on the dashed grey cluster box in the GeoDNS panel with the note the failed cluster keeps receiving traffic from stale caches. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: GeoDNS answers a name, anycast answers one address that routing steers.
alt: GeoDNS returns a regional IP that caches can keep stale, while anycast advertises one virtual IP from many locations and routing picks the nearest.
cap: GeoDNS returns a regional address that caches can keep stale, while anycast advertises one virtual address from many places and routing picks the nearest.

name: k35-gitops-fanout
title: A label on a new cluster is enough for the ApplicationSet to deploy to it
spec: A left-to-right flow in four stages. Stage 1 on the far left is a column of three registered cluster boxes labelled gpu-west, cpu-dev and gpu-east, where gpu-east is the new cluster and is highlighted green with a label chip gpu: true. Each box has a small cluster icon. Stage 2 is a filter box titled clusters generator with a monospace line selector matchLabels gpu: true, drawn as a funnel. The cpu-dev box has a dashed arrow ending at a grey X labelled not matched. Stage 3 is a template box titled ApplicationSet template with the monospace line name gpu-stack-{{name}} and the line server {{server}}, drawn as a stamp that is pressed once per matched cluster. Stage 4 is a column of Application boxes: gpu-stack-gpu-west and gpu-stack-gpu-east, each with an arrow pointing into a cluster box below labelled namespace gpu-system, with the monospace path clusters/{{metadata.labels.env}}/gpu-stack in a small note. Orange highlight on the gpu-east label chip with the note nobody logged in to the cluster. Under the flow a dashed return arrow from the stage 4 gpu-stack-gpu-east box back to stage 1, labelled if the label is removed, the generator stops producing it, and whether resources are removed depends on sync settings. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: the label does the work, and one template makes one Application per matching cluster.
alt: An ApplicationSet with a clusters generator makes one Application per cluster that carries the matching label, so a new labelled cluster is deployed automatically.
cap: An ApplicationSet produces one Application for each cluster that carries the matching label, so labelling a new cluster is enough to deploy to it.

name: k35-rings
title: Rings spread a change from a canary to all production, with a pause switch
spec: A horizontal sequence of four ring shapes drawn as nested or stepped boxes from left to right, each ring labelled by its name: ring 0 canary (note mirrors production hardware), ring 1 dev and staging, ring 2 prod ring 1 (note low-risk, the fewest users touched), ring 3 prod ring 2 (note the rest of production). Between each pair of rings a right arrow labelled soak time, with a small clock icon, meaning the change is watched before the next ring starts. Number circles r=24 green on each ring: 1 to 4. Above the rings, one long box at the top labelled pre-flight checks in CI, with three small items: API deprecation scan, Helm chart diff and admission policy tests, and a synthetic GPU job on the canary, drawn as a bar above ring 0. Below the rings a row of stop boxes: a rollback box labelled Git revert or node pool blue/green. Orange highlight on a global pause switch box placed at the bottom right, with a dashed arrow up into the arrow between ring 1 and ring 2 labelled stops the next ring before it starts. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: each ring must hold through its soak before the next one gets the change.
alt: A fleet change moves through rings from canary to production, with a soak time between rings and a global pause switch that stops the next ring.
cap: A fleet change moves ring by ring, from a canary to production, and each ring must hold through its soak time before the next one gets the change.

name: k35-mgmt-autoscaler
title: A management cluster that the workload cluster's autoscaler depends on
spec: Two layouts side by side. Left layout titled Central management cluster. alt: A central management cluster provisions workload clusters, and running the Cluster API components inside each workload cluster keeps autoscaling working without it.
cap: Running Cluster API inside each workload cluster keeps autoscaling working when the central management cluster is unavailable.
